newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin woos church, vexed by attacks on Nemtsov.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin woos church, vexed by attacks on Nemtsov.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, plunging back into the fray after a month-long vacation, on Wednesday began repairing ties with Russia's powerful Orthodox Church, hurt by his veto of a controversial law on religion.
Yeltsin, looking refreshed and confident as he parried reporters' questions, also said he was worried by attacks on his liberal protege, First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov.

The 66-year-old president returned to Moscow on Tuesday evening from the central region of Samara, where he spent the second half of his holiday fishing and receiving a steady stream of official visitors.

In his first public engagement he joined Patriarch Alexiy, head of the Orthodox Church, at the consecration ceremony of a small chapel dedicated to the medieval Saints Boris and Gleb on Arbat Square in central Moscow.
Yeltsin told the patriarch he fully recognised the church's central role in Russian history and said he would back a revised version of the law on religion which he vetoed last month.
The law, approved by both houses of parliament and strongly backed by the church, would have slapped tough restrictions on "non-traditional" religious groups and foreign missionaries.

Yeltsin rejected the bill in its current form, saying it contravened Russia's post-Soviet constitution which guarantees equality for all creeds. The United States, the Vatican and human rights groups had criticised the bill as discriminatory.

"A conciliatory commission will be set up with representatives from the church, the State Duma (lower house of parliament) the presidency and government," Yeltsin told reporters in televised remarks after the consecration ceremony.
"This commission will review all the articles of the bill and will remove those which are not compatible with the constitution. Then the law must be passed," he said.

Underlining the closer church-state ties that have developed since the fall of atheistic communism, Yeltsin was joined at Wednesday's ceremony by Defence Minister Igor Sergeyev, Security Council secretary Ivan Rybkin and other senior officials.
The new chapel has been raised on the site of a church destroyed by Soviet dictator Josef Stalin in the 1930s.

One of the most pressing issues awaiting Yeltsin's attention is the controversial sale of a controlling stake in Russian mining giant Norilsk Nickel against the wishes of Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and other senior officials.

The tender was won on Tuesday by a partner of commercial bank Uneximbank, which is already under fire from large sections of the mass media for winning a quarter stake in Russia's telecommunications company Svyazinvest last week.
The Svyazinvest sale pitted several powerful banking and media tycoons against Yeltsin's new liberal team led by First Deputy Prime Ministers Boris Nemtsov and Anatoly Chubais.
Nemtsov came under especially heavy attack in some sections of the media for his support of the sale.

"I cannot fail to be concerned about people I have promoted... we have now reached an agreement. There will be no more pressure," Interfax news agency quoted Yeltsin as saying on Wednesday. It gave no further details.
"Nemtsov must react patiently (to such attacks). The president also gets criticised but he stays calm," he added.
Yeltsin regards the young and charismatic Nemtsov as a possible heir.
Another urgent problem facing Yeltsin is the delicate peace process in breakaway Chechnya where Russian troops fought a bloody 21-month war against separatists that ended last August.

Chechen First Deputy Prime Minister Movladi Udugov told Interfax on Wednesday that Yeltsin would probably meet Chechnya's President Aslan Maskhadov in Moscow in mid-August to try to break a deadlock over a political treaty mapping out future relations between Russia and its unruly Caucasus region.
